lessons.title: Your Cyclical vs Defensive Checklist on Screener.in

body.text: Everything in this course collapses into one repeatable routine: pull ten years of numbers, place the business on the spectrum, normalise its earnings, price it honestly, and check how it fits what you already own. Thirty minutes per stock, and you never have to guess again.

children.text: This final lesson is the working version of the whole course. Nothing new, just the sequence, the exact places on Screener.in to find each number, and the thresholds to compare them against. Use the consolidated view unless a company's business is almost entirely in India, and keep the standalone view handy, since Chapter 2 showed how differently Tata Steel's Indian and consolidated numbers behaved.

body.text: Two traps from earlier chapters, worth remembering at this stage. A coefficient of variation slightly above 0.3 can simply mean the company grew steadily, as it did for HUL and Colgate, so read it alongside the decline years. And a collapse in ROCE can be caused by an acquisition adding capital rather than a business weakening, as with HUL after the GSK Consumer Healthcare merger. Always check the balance sheet before concluding a moat has broken.

body.caption: The same eight checks applied to two companies from this course, using figures from earlier lessons

children.text: History tells you how the business has behaved, not how it will. Screener.in's Documents section links annual reports and earnings call transcripts, and the Shareholding section shows whether institutions are entering or leaving. Read the last four earnings calls with three questions in mind: has a well-funded competitor arrived, has the industry consolidated or fragmented, and has anything in the balance sheet or business mix changed through acquisitions or demergers. Chapter 1 showed telecom moving across the spectrum on industry structure alone, and Chapter 4 showed a paints leader derating as a new entrant arrived.

body.caption: Shares outstanding is closely approximated by latest Net Profit divided by latest EPS

children.text: For a cyclical, this step is the difference between analysis and guesswork. Take the average and median OPM over 10 to 12 years, apply each to the latest year's revenue, subtract the latest depreciation and interest, apply the latest tax rate, and divide by the share count. Always calibrate: plug in the latest actual margin and check that your answer lands close to reported EPS. For a defensive with stable margins, normalising changes little, and your attention belongs on valuation instead.

body.title: Different Tools for Different Ends of the Spectrum

columns.label: For a cyclical

P/B, compared with its own history and with normalised ROE
EV/EBITDA using mid-cycle EBITDA, since EV includes debt
EV per tonne against the cost of building new capacity, where relevant

columns.label: For a defensive
points: P/E against the stock's own long-term median
Earnings yield against the 10-year government bond yield
ROCE durability, which is what the premium actually pays for
Years of expected growth needed to grow into the price

body.title: One Last Normalisation
body.prompt: A cyclical has revenue of ₹12,000 crore, a mid-cycle operating margin of 14%, depreciation of ₹500 crore, interest of ₹180 crore, a tax rate of 25%, and 60 crore shares. What is its normalised EPS in rupees? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Operating profit = 12,000 × 14% = ₹1,680 crore. Profit before tax = 1,680 - 500 - 180 = ₹1,000 crore. Net profit = 1,000 × 0.75 = ₹750 crore. Normalised EPS = 750 ÷ 60 = ₹12.50. If the current share price is ₹250, the normalised P/E is 20, whatever the headline P/E on peak earnings says.

children.text: Stage 5: Fit It to What You Already Own

A stock can pass every test above and still be wrong for you. Before buying, add it to your existing mix and check three things: what share of your equity would then sit on the cyclical end, whether your funds already hold it, and whether your income depends on the same cycle. A good cyclical bought by someone whose salary and employer stock ride the same cycle is a concentrated bet, however cheap it looks.

body.title: The 30-Minute Routine
steps: Open the company on Screener.in and choose the consolidated view, noting the standalone view if overseas operations are large
Copy 10 to 12 years of Sales, OPM %, Net Profit, and EPS from the Profit and Loss table into a sheet
Count loss years and decline years, note the worst fall, and calculate the OPM range and the coefficient of variation
Check Borrowings over 5 years in the Balance Sheet, and ROCE and the cash conversion cycle in the Ratios section
Place the company on the spectrum: deep cyclical, early cyclical, late cyclical, quasi-defensive, or true defensive
Scan the last four earnings calls in the Documents section for new competitors, capacity additions, or business mix changes
Calculate normalised EPS at the average and median margin, and calibrate against reported EPS
Value it with the right tools for its position on the spectrum, and compare with its own history
Check the fit: your target mix, overlap with your funds, and your income cyclicality
Write down the one thing that would prove you wrong, and diarise a review after the next annual results

body.text: Say no more often than yes. Most stocks fail at stage 4 because the price already reflects the good news, and quite a few fail at stage 5 because they duplicate exposure you already have. A routine that never produces a rejection is not a routine; it is a justification.

body.title: Where Does the Routine Usually Stop?
body.question: You run the full routine on a well-known cement company. Earnings history is clearly cyclical, competition is stable, and normalised EPS is ₹40 against a current share price of ₹1,200. Its 10-year median P/E on normalised earnings has been about 20. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: Buy, because the business quality is proven
At 30 times normalised earnings against a median of about 20, the price already assumes a lot, so this is a reject or a watchlist candidate
The P/E is irrelevant for cyclicals, so buy on the earnings history
Wait for the company to report record profits before buying
body.explanation: ₹1,200 ÷ ₹40 = 30 times normalised earnings, well above its own median of about 20. The business may be excellent, but the price leaves little room. Waiting for record profits would be worse, since that is exactly when cyclical earnings are at their peak.

cells: Glance at the macro dashboard from Chapter 5: PMI, vehicle sales, credit growth, GST, and IIP, noting direction rather than level
Check results for margin trends and any change in competitive commentary; rebalance if a sleeve has drifted more than about 5 percentage points
Re-run the full classification with the new year of data, and re-check your target mix against your horizon and income
Re-run immediately after a demerger, large acquisition, new entrant, or regulatory change

body.label: Screener.in
body.description: Profit and Loss, Balance Sheet, Cash Flow, Ratios, peer comparison, and links to annual reports and earnings call transcripts for every listed Indian company.

children.text: What This Course Was Really About

One idea has run through every chapter: judge a business by what happens to its earnings when the economy turns, not by what its share price did last year. That single discipline is what separated Tata Steel's four loss years from HUL's decade of steady growth, explained why a P/E of 3.3 was a warning rather than a bargain, and revealed why a consumption fund is not a defensive holding. You now have the measurements, the valuation tools, the macro dashboard, and a portfolio framework to apply it. The next cycle will look different in its details and identical in its structure.

body.label: If you remember one thing
body.value: Cyclical or defensive is a property of earnings, and price is a separate question
body.context: Get the classification from the earnings history, then decide separately whether the price is worth paying

points: Run the same five stages every time: classify, check what could change, normalise, value, and fit to your portfolio
Stage 1 needs only the Profit and Loss, Balance Sheet, and Ratios sections on Screener.in
Read ratios in context: steady growth inflates the coefficient of variation, and acquisitions depress ROCE
Use normalised earnings and asset-based measures for cyclicals, and median multiples and ROCE durability for defensives
A stock that passes every business test can still fail the portfolio test if it duplicates your existing exposure or your income risk
Re-run the classification annually and after any major corporate or industry event, since positions on the spectrum expire

body.text: Screener.in section names and features can change; use this as a guide rather than a literal map. Company figures are drawn from earlier lessons in this course, based on data available at the time of writing, and may be restated. Thresholds in the checklist are rules of thumb designed for teaching, not standards. The cyclical and cement examples are illustrative. This lesson is educational and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security, and it is not personalised investment advice.
